paragraphs: Another visitor, a lady, had been watching the elder talk with the peasants and bless them. She shed silent tears and dabbed them away with her handkerchief. She was a sentimental society lady, and in many respects a truly kind-hearted woman. When the elder finally came over to her, she met him with enthusiasm.

“Ah, what I felt as I watched that touching scene!...” She was too moved to go on. “Oh, I understand why the people love you so. I love the people myself. I want to love them. And who could not, our splendid Russian people, so simple in their greatness!”
“How is your daughter? You wanted to speak with me again?”

“Oh, I begged and begged for this, I prayed for it! I was ready to fall on my knees and stay there three days under your windows until you let me in. We have come, great healer, to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. You have healed my Lise, healed her completely, simply by praying over her last Thursday and laying your hands on her. We rushed here to kiss those hands, and to pour out our feelings and our reverence.”
“What do you mean, healed? She is still lying in her chair.”

“But the fevers she had at night have stopped altogether, every night since Thursday,” said the lady, nervous and hurried. “And that isn’t all. Her legs are stronger. This morning she got up feeling well, after sleeping the whole night through. Look at her rosy cheeks, her bright eyes! She used to cry constantly, and now she laughs, and she’s cheerful and happy. This morning she insisted that I let her stand, and she stood for a whole minute without anything to hold on to. She’s betting that in two weeks she’ll be dancing a quadrille. I called in Doctor Herzenstube. He shrugged and said, ‘I’m amazed; I can’t make anything of it.’ And you expect us not to come and trouble you? Not to fly here and thank you? Lise, thank him—thank him!”

Lise’s pretty, laughing little face turned suddenly serious. She lifted herself in her chair as high as she could, looked at the elder, and clasped her hands in front of him. Then she could not contain herself, and she burst out laughing.
“It’s at him,” she said, pointing at Alyosha. She was as cross with herself as a child for being unable to hold back her laughter.
If anyone had looked at Alyosha, standing a step behind the elder, he would have seen a quick blush flood his cheeks in an instant. His eyes shone, and he looked down.
“She has a message for you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How do you do?” the mother went on, and she held out her exquisitely gloved hand to Alyosha.
The elder turned around and suddenly studied Alyosha closely. Alyosha stepped nearer to Lise and, with a strangely awkward smile, held out his hand to her as well. Lise put on a solemn air.

“Katerina Ivanovna gave me this to pass on to you.” She handed him a little note. “She very much wants you to go and see her as soon as you possibly can. She asks that you not fail her, but be sure to come.”

“She wants me to come and see her? Me? Why?” Alyosha muttered in great astonishment. His face at once turned anxious. “Oh, it all has to do with Dmitri Fyodorovitch and—what happened recently,” the mother explained in a rush. “Katerina Ivanovna has come to a decision, but she needs to see you about it.... Why, naturally, I can’t say. But she wants to see you at once. And you will go to her, of course. It’s a Christian duty.”
“I’ve only met her once,” Alyosha protested, just as bewildered as before.

“Oh, she is such a noble, matchless creature! If only for what she has suffered.... Think of what she has gone through, and what she is going through now! Think of what lies ahead of her! It’s all terrible, terrible!”
“All right, I’ll come,” Alyosha decided, after a quick look at the short, baffling note. It was an urgent plea for him to come, and it explained nothing at all.

“Oh, how sweet and generous of you!” cried Lise, suddenly lively. “I told Mamma you’d be sure not to go. I said you were saving your soul. How wonderful you are! I’ve always thought you were wonderful. How glad I am to tell you so!”
“Lise!” said her mother severely, though she smiled as she said it.
“You have forgotten us altogether, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said. “You never come to see us. And yet Lise has told me twice that she’s never happy except with you.”

Alyosha raised his downcast eyes, blushed again, and again smiled without knowing why. But the elder was no longer watching him. He had started talking to a monk who, as I mentioned before, had been waiting for him beside Lise’s chair. This was plainly a monk of the humblest kind, which is to say a peasant, narrow in his outlook, but a true believer and, in his own way, a stubborn one. He said that he came from the far north, from Obdorsk, from Saint Sylvester, and that he belonged to a poor monastery with only ten monks. The elder blessed him and told him to come to his cell whenever he liked.
“How can you presume to do such deeds?” the monk asked suddenly, pointing at Lise with great solemnity and meaning. He was talking about her “healing.”

“It is much too early to speak of that, of course. Relief is not the same as a complete cure, and it can have different causes. But if there has been any healing, it came from no power but God’s will. It is all from God. Come and visit me, Father,” he added to the monk. “I cannot often receive visitors. I am ill, and I know my days are numbered.”
“Oh, no, no! God won’t take you from us. You’ll live a long, long time yet,” cried the lady. “And what is wrong with you? You look so well, so cheerful and happy.”

“Today I am remarkably better. But I know it will last only a moment. I understand my illness thoroughly now. If I seem happy to you, nothing you could say would please me more. For human beings are made for happiness, and whoever is completely happy has the right to say to himself, ‘I am doing God’s will on earth.’ All the righteous, all the saints, all the holy martyrs were happy.”

“Oh, how you talk! What bold, lofty words!” cried the lady. “Your words seem to pierce right through me. And yet—happiness, happiness—where is it? Who can say of himself that he is happy? Oh, since you have been kind enough to let us see you once more today, let me tell you what I could not say last time, what I did not dare to say, everything I suffer and have suffered for so long! I am suffering! Forgive me! I am suffering!”
And in a surge of passionate feeling she clasped her hands before him.
“What is it, in particular, that you suffer from?”
“I suffer ... from lack of faith.”
“Lack of faith in God?”

“Oh, no, no! I don’t even dare to think of that. But the life to come—it’s such a riddle! And no one, no one can solve it. Listen! You are a healer, you know the human soul so deeply, and of course I can’t expect you to believe me entirely. But I give you my word of honor that I’m not speaking lightly now. The thought of the life beyond the grave drives me to anguish, to terror. And I don’t know whom to ask, and I never have dared, all my life. And now I’m bold enough to ask you. Oh, God! What will you think of me now?”
She wrung her hands.
“Do not worry about what I think of you,” said the elder. “I fully believe that your suffering is sincere.”

“Oh, how grateful I am to you! You see, I shut my eyes and ask myself: if everyone has faith, where did it come from? And then people do say it all comes from terror of the threatening forces of nature, and that none of it is real. And I say to myself, ‘What if I’ve believed all my life, and when I come to die there’s nothing but burdocks growing on my grave?’ as I read in some author. It’s dreadful! How—how can I get my faith back? But I only believed when I was a small child, mechanically, without thinking about anything. How, how is it to be proved? I’ve come now to lay my soul open to you and ask you about it. If I let this chance go by, no one will ever answer me, not in my whole life. How can I prove it? How can I convince myself? Oh, how unhappy I am! I stand and look around me and see that hardly anyone else cares. No one bothers his head about it, and I’m the only one who can’t stand it. It’s deadly—deadly!”
“No doubt. But there is no proving it, though you can be convinced of it.”
“How?”

“Through the experience of active love. Try to love your neighbor actively and without tiring. The further you go in love, the more certain you will be that God exists and that your soul is immortal. If you reach complete self-forgetfulness in loving your neighbor, then you will believe without doubt, and no doubt can enter your soul. This has been tried. This is certain.”

“In active love? Now that’s another question—and what a question! You see, I love humanity so much that—would you believe it?—I often dream of giving up everything I have, leaving Lise, and becoming a sister of mercy. I close my eyes and think and dream, and at that moment I feel strong enough to overcome any obstacle. No wounds, no festering sores could frighten me then. I would bind them up and wash them with my own hands. I would nurse the afflicted. I would be ready to kiss their wounds.”
“That is a great deal, and it is good that your mind is full of such dreams and not others. One day, without noticing, you may really do a good deed.”

“Yes. But could I stand such a life for long?” the lady went on, fervent, almost frantic. “That’s the main question—that’s the question that torments me most. I shut my eyes and ask myself, ‘Would you keep going on that path for long? And what if the patient whose wounds you were washing did not meet you with gratitude? What if he pestered you with his whims, never valued or even noticed your charity, abused you and bossed you rudely, and complained about you to the authorities (which often happens when people are in great pain)—what then? Would you keep on loving, or not?’ And do you know, I reached a horrifying conclusion. If anything could kill my love for humanity, it would be ingratitude. In short, I’m a hired servant. I expect my wages at once—that is, praise, and love paid back with love. Otherwise I can’t love anyone.”
She was in a perfect frenzy of self-punishment, and when she finished she looked at the elder with defiant resolve.

“That is just the story a doctor once told me,” observed the elder. “He was getting on in years, and undoubtedly a clever man. He spoke as frankly as you do, though in jest, in bitter jest. ‘I love humanity,’ he said, ‘but I am surprised at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love people one at a time. In my dreams,’ he said, ‘I have often made rapturous plans to serve humanity, and I might even have gone to the cross for it, had that suddenly been required. And yet I cannot share a room with anyone for two days running, as I know from experience. The moment anyone is near me, his personality offends my self-importance and cramps my freedom. In twenty-four hours I begin to hate the best of men: one because he takes too long over his dinner, another because he has a cold and keeps blowing his nose. I turn hostile to people the moment they come close. But it has always happened that the more I hate people one by one, the more ardent my love for humanity becomes.’”
“But what is to be done? What can one do in such a case? Must one despair?”

“No. It is enough that it distresses you. Do what you can, and it will be counted to your credit. A great deal is already done in you, since you can know yourself so deeply and honestly. But suppose you have been talking to me so frankly only to win praise for your frankness, as you did from me just now. Then of course you will get nowhere in achieving real love. It will never go beyond dreams, and your whole life will slip away like a phantom. In that case you will naturally stop thinking about the future life too, and in the end you will calm down on your own, after a fashion.”

“You have crushed me! Only now, as you speak, do I see that I was really only angling for your praise of my sincerity when I said I couldn’t bear ingratitude. You have shown me myself. You have seen through me and explained me to myself!”

“Are you telling the truth? Well, then, after such a confession I believe that you are sincere and good at heart. If you do not find happiness, always remember that you are on the right road, and try not to leave it. Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness toward yourself. Watch your own deceitfulness and examine it every hour, every minute. Avoid scorn, toward others and toward yourself. What seems bad in you will grow purer simply because you see it in yourself. Avoid fear too, though fear is only the consequence of every sort of falsehood. Never be frightened by your own weakness in pursuing love. Do not be too frightened even by your evil actions. I am sorry I can say nothing more consoling to you, for love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, quickly done and seen by all. People will even give their lives, if only the trial does not last long but is soon over, with everyone watching and applauding as if at a play. But active love is labor and endurance, and for some people, perhaps, a whole science. But I predict that just when you see with horror that, in spite of all your efforts, you are moving farther from your goal and not closer to it—at that very moment, I predict, you will reach it. You will see clearly the miraculous power of the Lord, who has loved you all along and has been guiding you in secret. Forgive me, I cannot stay longer with you. They are waiting for me. Goodbye.”
The lady was weeping.
“Lise, Lise! Bless her—bless her!” she cried, jumping up suddenly.
“She does not deserve your love. I have seen her naughtiness the whole time,” the elder said teasingly. “Why were you laughing at Alexey?”

In fact Lise had spent the whole time mocking him. She had noticed earlier that Alyosha was shy and tried not to look at her, and she found this extremely funny. She waited intently to catch his eye. Alyosha could not bear her fixed stare. Suddenly, helplessly, he was pulled into glancing at her, and at once she smiled at him in triumph. Alyosha was more flustered and vexed than ever. At last he turned away from her completely and hid behind the elder’s back. A few minutes later, drawn by the same irresistible force, he turned again to see whether she was looking at him. He found Lise nearly hanging out of her chair to peep at him from the side, eagerly waiting for him to look. When she caught his eye, she laughed so much that the elder could not help saying, “Why do you make fun of him like that, you naughty girl?”
Lise suddenly, quite unexpectedly, blushed. Her eyes flashed and her face turned quite serious. She began to speak fast and nervously, in a hot, resentful voice:

“Why has he forgotten everything, then? He used to carry me around when I was little. We used to play together. He used to come and teach me to read, you know. Two years ago, when he went away, he said he would never forget me, that we were friends for ever, for ever, for ever! And now all of a sudden he’s afraid of me. Am I going to eat him? Why won’t he come near me? Why won’t he talk? Why won’t he come and visit us? It’s not that you won’t let him. We know he goes everywhere. It isn’t proper for me to invite him. He should have thought of it first, if he hasn’t forgotten me. No, now he’s saving his soul! Why did you put that long gown on him? If he runs, he’ll fall.”

And suddenly she hid her face in her hand and burst into helpless, long, nervous laughter that made no sound. The elder listened to her with a smile and blessed her tenderly. As she kissed his hand, she suddenly pressed it to her eyes and began to cry.
“Don’t be angry with me. I’m silly and good for nothing ... and maybe Alyosha is right, quite right, not to want to come and see such a ridiculous girl.”
“I will certainly send him to you,” said the elder.
